title: Who has the most at stake in 2026?
channel_name: The Athletic Football Show: A show about the NFL
text: Every single person in the NFL—players, head coaches, coordinators, position coaches, executives, you name it—has something at stake every season. But some people have more at stake in one individual season than most everyone else. So who has the most at stake in 2026? Robert Mays, Derrik Klassen and Dave Helman answer that question on this episode of The Athletic Football Show. title: Broncos RB Preview — Dobbins’ Healthy, Harvey’s Encore & Coleman’s Ready | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews conclude with a deep dive into the Broncos running backs, a room loaded with talent, versatility, and major 2026 expectations. JK Dobbins is the starter and the clear lead back — explosive, efficient, and the centerpiece of the run game. But how much more playing time does RJ Harvey get this year. Harvey scored 12 touchdowns as a rookie, proving he’s more than just a change‑of‑pace option. What does he do for an encore in Year 2. Does he push for a bigger slice of the workload. Then there’s Jonah Coleman — the talented rookie who can be relied on as a full‑time back if Dobbins gets hurt again. Coleman’s power, balance, and vision make him one of the most important insurance policies on the roster. This RB room is deep, dynamic, and absolutely central to the Broncos’ offensive identity in 2026. 🔥 In this episode: Why Dobbins remains the unquestioned RB1 How Harvey builds on a 12‑TD rookie season Why Coleman is a plug‑and‑play starter if needed How Davis Webb’s offense maximizes all three backs What the rotation could look like once camp begins Drop your take — who leads the Broncos in touchdowns this season. title: 5 Smartest Broncos Offseason Moves — Blueprint to Win a Super Bowl | Orange & Blue Today
text: It’s a solo Thursday edition of Orange & Blue Today, and Cecil Lammey is breaking down the 5 SMARTEST moves of the Broncos offseason — the decisions that didn’t just improve the roster… they built a legitimate Super Bowl blueprint for 2026. First, the blockbuster: Trading for Jaylen Waddle and a 2026 4th. Denver gave up a 1st, 3rd, and 4th — but landed a superstar WR1 who changes spacing, changes coverages, and changes the entire math of the offense. This is the kind of move contenders make. Then the retention moves that matter: Re‑signing JK Dobbins (2 years, $20M) keeps the run game explosive and stable. Re‑signing Justin Strnad (3 years, $18M) locks in one of the most underrated defenders in the league — a leader, communicator, and turnover creator. The draft brought juice too: Selecting Jonah Coleman gives Denver a plug‑and‑play back who can carry the load if needed and add real pop behind Dobbins and Harvey. And finally, the organizational foundation: Extensions for George Paton and Sean Payton stabilize the franchise, align the long‑term vision, and ensure the Broncos aren’t just building for 2026 — they’re building a multi‑year window. These five moves weren’t random. They were intentional. Strategic. Championship‑minded. And Cecil breaks down exactly why they matter. 🔥 In this episode: Why the Waddle trade is a Super Bowl‑level swing How Dobbins’ deal keeps the offense balanced and dangerous Why Strnad’s extension is quietly elite roster building How Jonah Coleman strengthens the RB room instantly Why Paton & Payton extensions create a real championship window Drop your take — which move was the smartest, and which one pushes Denver closest to a Super Bowl.

title: Broncos OT Preview — Bolles’ & McGlinchey star bookends, Crum's future spot? | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews roll into Wednesday with a deep dive into the Broncos offensive tackles, a group that’s strong right now but full of long‑term questions. Garett Bolles remains a franchise left tackle — durable, athletic, and still playing at a high level. But how much longer can he maintain that standard. With age and contract realities looming, Mase and Cecil break down what Bolles’ future looks like and how the Broncos prepare for life after him. That leads directly to Frank Crum, the developmental monster with size, movement skills, and real upside. The big question: Is Crum the future at left tackle… or right tackle. His traits fit both spots, and Wednesday’s show digs into where he projects best — and how soon he might be ready. On the right side, Mike McGlinchey continues to be outstanding — powerful in the run game, steady in pass protection, and a veteran leader. But like Bolles, he’s a seasoned vet, and the Broncos must start thinking about the future at RT as well. This tackle group is strong today, but the long‑term picture is where things get fascinating. 🔥 In this episode: How much longer Bolles can play at a high level Whether Frank Crum is the future at LT or RT What McGlinchey’s veteran status means for the RT timeline How the Broncos plan succession at both tackle spots Why the OT room is critical to Bo Nix’s 2026 ceiling Drop your take — who’s the Broncos’ long‑term answer at tackle. title: Broncos EDGE Preview — Bonitto’s Strip‑Sack Jump, & Elliss Breaking Out | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews continue — and Monday’s show is all about the Broncos EDGE rushers, the group Vance Joseph is counting on to fuel the defense’s push for more turnovers in 2026. Nik Bonitto has already become one of the NFL’s most dangerous pure pass rushers — bend, burst, and finishing ability. But can he take the next step and turn pressures into more strip‑sacks. With VJ demanding more takeaways, Bonitto is the player most capable of delivering them. Behind him, Que Robinson keeps flashing legit pass‑rush juice. The question is simple: How does Que get more playing time. title: Broncos CB Preview — Surtain’s INT Jump, Moss’ Contract‑Year Stakes | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews continue — and today Mase and Cec break down one of the deepest, most fascinating groups on the roster: the Broncos cornerbacks. At the top sits Pat Surtain — arguably the best cornerback in the NFL. But with Vance Joseph hammering the message of more turnovers, can Surtain boost his interception total in 2026. He’s elite in coverage, but can he turn more of those shutdown reps into game‑changing takeaways. Across from him, Riley Moss enters a contract year. His improved play last season was undeniable — but if he continues that rise, does he earn a payday the Broncos may not be able to match. Moss’ 2026 season could reshape the future of the CB room. Then comes the mystery piece: Jahdae Barron. The 2025 first‑round pick has talent, versatility, and toughness — but what is his position. Is he a boundary corner who can push Moss. Or is he a slot defender. And if he’s a slot, can he realistically push JaQuan McMillian — one of the best nickel corners in the league. Or is Barron simply a gifted player who must wait behind three quality starters until a spot opens. Finally, Kris Abrams‑Draine enters the conversation as a developmental CB with intriguing long‑term upside. What does his future look like in a crowded room. This CB group is loaded with talent, layered with questions, and absolutely central to Vance Joseph’s turnover‑driven identity. 🔥 In this episode: Why Surtain could finally see an interception jump in 2026 How Moss’ contract year shapes the future of the CB room Whether Barron is a boundary corner, a slot defender, or a long‑term chess piece If McMillian’s elite slot play blocks Barron’s path to snaps What the Broncos envision for Kris Abrams‑Draine moving forward

title: Broncos Battles: Troy Franklin vs. Pat Bryant — Who Wins WR3 Battle in 2026 | Orange & Blue Today
text: It’s a special VERSUS edition of Orange & Blue Today, and Cecil Lammey goes solo to break down one of the most important camp battles on the entire roster: Troy Franklin vs. Pat Bryant for the Broncos’ No. 3 wide receiver job. Franklin enters Year 3 with a résumé full of mixed results — an early‑season surge in 2025 followed by a late‑season fade that left big questions about consistency, physicality, and trust. Can he stabilize his game and reclaim the momentum he flashed last fall. Bryant, meanwhile, is entering Year 2 with true “X” receiver upside — size, strength, and clutch‑catch ability that mirrors the role Courtland Sutton currently owns. The big question: Is Bryant more than just a waiting receiver behind Sutton. Could his frame, toughness, and reliability secure him the WR3 job outright. And with Davis Webb calling plays, the WR3 role changes dramatically. Targets will be spread among Evan Engram, RJ Harvey, and the top two receivers — Jaylen Waddle (superstar WR1) and Sutton (the consistent outside force). So who fits the offense better. Who earns the trust. Who wins the job. This battle is real. It’s close.
